item.title: PHP2Shell exploited against firewalls
item.description:
CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (PHP2Shell) are actively exploited against PAN-OS firewalls. A China-nexus actor chained them with a kernel privesc to root 25 firewalls including U.S. 🇺🇸 government systems.
Key findings:
- PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) allows unauthenticated RCE via a single malicious multipart HTTP request against the PAN-OS management web interface and XML API, no credentials or user interaction required. Palo Alto Networks assigned a product-specific severity score of 8.7 (High). Affected releases span PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1, 12.2, and Panorama. Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 (advisory SSA-566512) is also in scope. Both CVEs are now actively exploited and CISA added chained kernel privesc CVE-2026-46300 (Fragnesia) to KEV on October 28.
- The appliance exploitation advantage is real: public PHP2Shell exploits fail against default servers because memory offsets vary per build. Firmware-bundled PHP removes that obstacle entirely. Every device on the same firmware version runs the same PHP 8.0.30 build with a high memory limit, making a version-tuned exploit reliable at scale. The PHP worker process may also hold passwords, tokens, API keys, and certificates from in-flight requests that an attacker can read from memory.
- A suspected China-nexus actor used FOFA to enumerate exposed management interfaces, filtered to vulnerable firmware versions, then automated exploitation. Post-compromise activity included web shell deployment, reverse SSH tunnels, LDAP service account credential theft, password spraying, and AD reconnaissance. The actor reached an internal management server accessible only through a VPN tunnel the compromised firewall terminated, affecting 25 firewalls across the United States 🇺🇸, Japan 🇯🇵, Taiwan 🇹🇼, and South Korea 🇰🇷.
- Patching closes the PHP flaw but leaves post-exploitation artifacts in place. Indicators to hunt on compromised devices include unexpected outbound SSH connections, web shells on the management interface, unusual administrative account activity, LDAP service account credential use, and AD password spraying or new account creation. Firewall logs forwarded to a SIEM before compromise are your only reliable source: an attacker with root can clear appliance-local logs.
Takeaway: PAN-OS 12.2 requires 12.2.4-h1 or later; other branches need the per-maintenance-release hotfix. Before assuming a clean state post-patch, hunt for web shells on the management interface, review outbound SSH from the firewall, audit your LDAP service account for unauthorized binds, and check AD for password spraying and new accounts. If management logs were not forwarded to a SIEM prior to compromise, treat the appliance as potentially tampered. IOCs and campaign detail are in the Dream and Field Effect reports.

item.title: Supabase From a Pentester's Perspective: Methodology and Where the Real Risks Hide
item.description:
Supabase's direct-to-client database model shifts the authorization burden entirely to developers. Missing Row Level Security (RLS) or exposed privileged keys can hand attackers direct REST access to production data.
Key findings:
- The attack surface starts in JavaScript and mobile app bundles. Pentesters hunt for Supabase project URLs (ending in .supabase[.]co), createClient() initialization code, anon or publishable keys, JWT tokens, and references to table or bucket names. The anon key in client code is expected by design, but a service_role or secret key exposed client-side bypasses RLS entirely and effectively grants unrestricted database access. That is a hard line: if a privileged key lands in frontend code, treat it as a full compromise of the data layer.
- The core exploit path is simple: issue an unauthenticated GET to /rest/v1/<table-name> against a project where RLS is disabled or misconfigured. If the table is readable, every row comes back. The report references the Moltbook incident as a public, real-world example where an exposed anon key plus missing RLS led to unrestricted access to sensitive data at scale, including millions of stored API keys. Other high-value endpoints to probe are /auth/v1/ for authentication flows, /storage/v1/ for file buckets, /functions/v1/ for Edge Functions, and /graphql/v1 when GraphQL is enabled.
- Authorization testing must cover all four CRUD operations, not just SELECT. A table that correctly restricts reads can still expose a writeable INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE policy. The same logic extends to storage buckets: a bucket that blocks object listing may still allow direct reads of files with predictable names, plus unauthorized uploads or overwrites. An empty array response does not confirm RLS is working. Confirming requires writing a known record as user A and attempting retrieval as user B or unauthenticated.
- Beyond broken access control, the report flags several compounding issues defenders often overlook: missing rate limits on login and password reset endpoints, JWT or session tokens stored in localStorage or sessionStorage (XSS becomes a full API compromise because the token grants direct database and storage access), injection risks in Edge Functions that run with elevated service_role privileges, and expensive unthrottled queries that can be abused for application-layer denial of service even when data access is restricted.
- Supabase separates logs across API, database, authentication, storage, Realtime, and Edge Function layers. No single event flags enumeration. The pattern is what matters: repeated requests across table names, broad "select=*" queries, authorization failures in sequence, unusual data volumes, or privileged function calls outside expected flows.
Practitioner takeaway: if you are hunting for Supabase exposure in your environment, correlate API logs with auth and storage logs looking for sequential 200 responses across varied table names from a single source, broad column selection requests, and authorization failures spiking from unauthenticated origins. Check your client-side bundles and mobile apps for service_role or secret key strings now, before a pentester does. item.content:encoded:
Supabase's direct-to-client database model shifts the authorization burden entirely to developers. Missing Row Level Security (RLS) or exposed privileged keys can hand attackers direct REST access to production data.

Key findings:

- The attack surface starts in JavaScript and mobile app bundles. Pentesters hunt for Supabase project URLs (ending in .supabase[.]co), createClient() initialization code, anon or publishable keys, JWT tokens, and references to table or bucket names. The anon key in client code is expected by design, but a service_role or secret key exposed client-side bypasses RLS entirely and effectively grants unrestricted database access. That is a hard line: if a privileged key lands in frontend code, treat it as a full compromise of the data layer.

- The core exploit path is simple: issue an unauthenticated GET to /rest/v1/<table-name> against a project where RLS is disabled or misconfigured. If the table is readable, every row comes back. The report references the Moltbook incident as a public, real-world example where an exposed anon key plus missing RLS led to unrestricted access to sensitive data at scale, including millions of stored API keys. Other high-value endpoints to probe are /auth/v1/ for authentication flows, /storage/v1/ for file buckets, /functions/v1/ for Edge Functions, and /graphql/v1 when GraphQL is enabled.

- Authorization testing must cover all four CRUD operations, not just SELECT. A table that correctly restricts reads can still expose a writeable INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE policy. The same logic extends to storage buckets: a bucket that blocks object listing may still allow direct reads of files with predictable names, plus unauthorized uploads or overwrites. An empty array response does not confirm RLS is working. Confirming requires writing a known record as user A and attempting retrieval as user B or unauthenticated.

- Beyond broken access control, the report flags several compounding issues defenders often overlook: missing rate limits on login and password reset endpoints, JWT or session tokens stored in localStorage or sessionStorage (XSS becomes a full API compromise because the token grants direct database and storage access), injection risks in Edge Functions that run with elevated service_role privileges, and expensive unthrottled queries that can be abused for application-layer denial of service even when data access is restricted.

- Supabase separates logs across API, database, authentication, storage, Realtime, and Edge Function layers. No single event flags enumeration. The pattern is what matters: repeated requests across table names, broad "select=*" queries, authorization failures in sequence, unusual data volumes, or privileged function calls outside expected flows.

Practitioner takeaway: if you are hunting for Supabase exposure in your environment, correlate API logs with auth and storage logs looking for sequential 200 responses across varied table names from a single source, broad column selection requests, and authorization failures spiking from unauthenticated origins. Check your client-side bundles and mobile apps for service_role or secret key strings now, before a pentester does. The report's defensive checklist and the Supabase Security Advisor dashboard are your baseline verification starting points.

item.title: Yoba Malware Hides a Crypto Miner Behind Legitimate OpenAI and Anthropic Binaries
item.description:
Yoba malware abuses signed OpenAI and Anthropic binaries to sideload a crypto miner, using Telegram, DNS-over-HTTPS, and Catbox to route around traditional C2 detection, active since at least June 2026.
Key findings:
- The infection chain starts with SEO-poisoned fake GitHub repositories posing as AI desktop apps (GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus). Each ZIP contains a legitimate signed Setup.exe from OpenAI or Anthropic alongside a malicious winmm.dll compiled the same day the archive was created. DLL sideloading means the signed binary loads the malicious DLL on its own, giving the chain an unusually clean appearance. No password protection was needed because the binaries had low detection rates via anti-sandbox techniques before security tools could unpack and examine them.
- YobaDropper hashes the name of the launching process and only proceeds if it equals Setup.exe. If that check fails, it does not exit cleanly: it loops a sleep of 5.5 seconds 200,000 times, stalling sandbox analysis for roughly 12.73 days. It also checks keyboard layout and skips CIS-region victims across Russian 🇷🇺, Belarusian 🇧🇾, Tajik, Armenian, Azerbaijani, Georgian, Kazakh 🇰🇿, Kyrgyz, Turkmen, Uzbek, and Tatar layouts. Ukraine 🇺🇦 is not excluded. The dropper then copies the legitimate WMPDMC.exe from System32 into a new ProgramData\WMProcess folder and drops wmpdui.dll there as a second-stage payload.
- Persistence is a scheduled task disguised as a Microsoft Windows Media Player metadata collector, authored as Microsoft Corporation, running as Local System three minutes after boot. It launches the legitimate WMPDMC.exe, which sideloads wmpdui.dll as YobaLoader. The loader contacts t[.]me/yoba_fanclub on Telegram, pulls the channel's profile picture, seeds the last 50 bytes into a domain generation algorithm producing adjective-noun-verb-number patterns on dedyn[.]io, then queries Google DNS-over-HTTPS (dns[.]google) for a TXT record on the generated domain. The response is signed and decrypted to yield a Catbox payload link. Changing the Telegram profile picture rotates the active domain instantly with no traditional C2 infrastructure involved.
- The final payload is XMRig 6.26.0, injected into svchost.exe, mining via a TLS-enabled onion endpoint through a local Tor SOCKS5 proxy. The miner bundles Tor 0.4.9.12 and lyrebird 0.8.1, uses roughly 85% of CPU threads, pauses on user input, resumes after 240 seconds of inactivity, and can load the WinRing0 driver service for MSR-based optimization. Critically, YobaLoader's DNS tasking system accepts any PE or PowerShell payload, so this infrastructure is not limited to mining.
- Earlier June 2026 variants used Cursor.exe for sideloading, a startup shortcut for persistence, excluded only Russia 🇷🇺, and resolved through .aber[.]ir instead of dedyn[.]io. The evolution from that version to the current one, which dropped anti-VM and anti-debugging checks in favor of the parent-process hash check and the sleep loop, shows active development and an operator refining evasion trade-offs over time.
Hunt for WMPDMC.exe running from any path outside System32, scheduled tasks with Microsoft Corporation as author that launch from ProgramData, DoH queries to dns[.]google resolving dedyn[.]io subdomains, outbound connections to t[.]me from non-browser processes, and svchost.exe instances with unexplained high CPU that have no standard service hosting them. IOCs are in the Check Point report.

item.title: Detection Engineering: Implementing Detection-as-Code in an Existing Environment: Part 1: Introduction and Concept
item.description:
Detection-as-Code migration in a live environment: NVISO's case study shows how to restructure a fragmented detection library into a per-detection repository model without halting operations or breaking existing Splunk deployments.
Key findings:
- The starting environment had detection data scattered across multiple Git repos, a file share holding YAML metadata, and Excel sheets, with Atomic Red Team tests grouped by MITRE ATT&CK technique rather than by individual detection. A single detection change could require multiple pull requests across separate repos plus a manual file-share update, making review error-prone and audit trails unreliable. Splunk savedsearches.conf files ran into thousands of lines covering unrelated detections, including configuration blocks for retired rules that were never cleaned up.
- The target structure collapses everything into one detection repository organized around the detection as the atomic unit. Each detection gets its own folder (e.g., DET00001/) containing meta.yml, test-atomic.yml, and platform-specific config blocks (splunk-searches.conf, splunk-transforms.conf, splunk-macros.conf, and lookup CSVs). Platform repos still exist but only hold deployment logic, not detection definitions. Retiring a detection becomes a folder move from detections/ to detections_retired/, which is both traceable and reversible in Git history.
- The migration required a deliberate sequencing: fix malformed YAML before scripting anything, build tooling to regenerate platform configs from the new structure, merge in-flight work before the freeze, then execute a single-day freeze on main branches. Feature branches in progress had to be recreated against the new repo rather than rebased, and old branches were deleted unmerged. The Atomic Red Team test split (removing technique-level test cases that did not belong to a specific detection) was intentionally deferred because it had no impact on platform deployment.
- A YAML validator was built as both a CLI tool and a pipeline gate. Integrated into the build pipeline, it blocks pull requests that introduce schema violations or inconsistencies, locking in the data quality gains made during migration. This is the foundation the report identifies as the prerequisite for automated compliance report generation, coverage analysis, and further integrations.
Practitioner takeaway: if your detection library has the same fragmentation pattern (metadata in one place, logic in another, tests in a third), the structural model here is worth adopting. The migration sequence matters as much as the target state: validate and fix YAML first, script and test the restructuring against a copy, minimize the freeze window, and handle in-flight branches explicitly. The report covers the roadmap in Part 1; Part 2 addresses Git history preservation and post-migration cleanup, which are the steps most teams underestimate.

item.title: Re: CVE-2026-102508: Apache PLC4X: OPC UA secure channel: integrity bypass, unverifiable server certificate, and silent downgrade
item.description:
CVE-2026-102508 and CVE-2026-102509 in Apache PLC4X allow a rogue OPC UA server to silently strip integrity protections, harvest credentials, and falsify PLC values with no client-side error. Fixed only in 1.0.0; most downstream consumers still pin vulnerable releases.
Key details:
- CVE-2026-102508 (PLC4X 0.9.0 - 0.13.1) chains three defects in the OPC UA secure channel. In AsymmetricEncryptionHandler.verify(), a missing negation inverts the signature check so any bytes, including zeros or random data, pass as valid. In BaseEncryptionHandler.decodeMessage(), the post-decryption (shorter) buffer is verified against the original on-wire length, feeding verify() a misaligned slice that never matches, and bug 1 silently accepts that failure. The default trust configuration compounds this: with no trust-store-file, OpcuaDriverContext accepted any certificate from the unauthenticated GetEndpoints response, encrypting the client nonce and user password to an attacker-supplied key. A downgrade defect (0.12.0+) also admits a weaker security policy when only one of policy or mode mismatches, and from 0.13.0 sorts admitted candidates ascending by securityLevel, preferring the weakest. The researcher demonstrated this in full: a relay answered GetEndpoints with its own certificate, decrypted the client OPN, derived the symmetric session keys, and altered a write from 100.0 to 999.0 confirmed on the real server, with zero error at the client.
- CVE-2026-102509 (0.10.0 - 0.13.1) covers three pre-authentication denial-of-service paths. PascalByteString.staticParse() allocates a byte array from a signed int32 wire length before checking availability; setting senderCertificate.stringLength to FF FF FF 7F in an 88-byte OPN response triggers OutOfMemoryError on the Netty thread repeatedly as the client retries. FieldReaderArray.readFieldCount() bounds against Integer.MAX_VALUE only, then pre-allocates an ArrayList backing array before reading any element; a Variant with count 0x7FFFFFFF attempts a multi-gigabyte allocation, reachable in CreateSessionResponse before ActivateSession. Third, Conversation never enforces negotiated maxChunkCount or maxMessageSize on receive; streaming 2,000 MSG chunks of 61,440 bytes (~120 MB) with the continue flag and no final chunk exhausts the JVM, exiting only if -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError is set. The byte-array allocator is in the shared plc4j-spi and affects ADS and OPC UA drivers specifically.
- Downstream exposure is broad. Apache Camel camel-plc4x bundles PLC4X 0.13.1 in its current release (4.23.0) and all active LTS lines; Camel main merged the 1.0.0 update (CAMEL-25617, 2026-10-27) but has not shipped a release yet. Apache StreamPipes 0.98.0 carries 0.13.1 with OPC UA excluded but ADS present, exposing SPI defects. Apache HertzBeat 1.8.0 and 1.9.0 carry 0.12.0 with Modbus and S7 drivers, bounded by their narrower field widths. Roughly a dozen smaller OT gateways and PLC bridges pin 0.9.0 - 0.13.1. Against a Camel route, a rogue server can harvest OPC UA credentials and push falsified values to a historian, database, or message topic with no error surface.
- Commits a2dbb6bfc0 and 5a4d5bdb4c (2026-07-10) restore the signature negation, pass the post-decrypt length to verify(), fail the certificate verifier closed by default, enforce chunk count and message size limits, and cap array initial capacity at 1024. Commit 372501287d (2026-06-12) rewrites the SPI read buffer to check availability before allocating. All three ship only in PLC4X 1.0.0, which also defaults to Basic256Sha256 with SignAndEncrypt and rejects weaker negotiated policies. Adding a trust-store-file on pre-1.0.0 deployments blocks certificate impersonation but does not fix the OPN signature check or the byte-string allocation trigger.
Responder action: inventory every application pulling plc4j-driver-opcua or plc4j-driver-all, including transitive Camel, StreamPipes, and HertzBeat dependencies. Until upgrade to 1.0.0, configure a trust-store-file to limit certificate impersonation. For threat-hunting, look for OPC UA sessions that completed without a client-side error but where the connecting server certificate differs from the expected endpoint certificate, and correlate historian or database writes for values inconsistent with physical process state. The full write-up and timeline are at the researcher's post linked in the OSS-Security thread.

item.title: Trojanized Claude Code extension distributed through Cursor marketplace
item.description:
Trojanized Claude Code extension version 2.1.313 was distributed through the Cursor marketplace for roughly 11 hours on October 29, 2026, exposing up to 5,000 developers to an SSH backdoor and credential harvesting loader with cross-platform persistence.
Key details:
- The attack was supply chain abuse, not a software vulnerability. A malicious build was published under Anthropic's legitimate extension identifier in the Cursor marketplace between 2:27am and 1:35pm PT on October 29. A 66-line loader was injected ahead of the legitimate code in extension.js and executed automatically on extension load with no user interaction required. The Microsoft VS Code Marketplace, Open VSX, and npm distributions are not confirmed to have delivered the malicious version.
- The loader performs several hostile actions on installation: it collects hostnames, usernames, OS details, working directories, Git config, public IPs, and the names of environment variables associated with credentials and cloud services. It adds an adversary-controlled SSH key named svc-telemetry to authorized_keys, attempts to enable the local SSH service, and tries to establish a reverse SSH tunnel to 134.209.82[.]225 on ports 22 and 8099. Errors in the malicious code prevent the full SSH backdoor from functioning on most Windows and macOS systems unless Cursor runs with administrator privileges, but the key is written, persistence is installed, and host data is transmitted regardless.
- Platform-specific persistence is installed on all three operating systems: a LaunchAgent named com[.]apple.sysmond on macOS, a scheduled task named SysMon on Windows, and cron-based entries on Linux. The svc-telemetry SSH key remains active after the extension is removed or updated. A Linux workstation running SSH and reachable over VPN stays accessible to whoever holds the matching private key until that key is explicitly deleted from authorized_keys.
- The primary risk is not the workstation itself but everything reachable from it. Developers whose Cursor sessions had access to production cloud environments, source code repositories, CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure management systems, or privileged credentials represent the highest-impact exposure. The loader does not fetch additional payloads, but no public report rules out follow-on access for hosts where the SSH tunnel did establish successfully.
Practitioner takeaway: Scope starts with installation logs. Identify hosts that installed or updated Claude Code from the Cursor marketplace during the 2:27am to 1:35pm PT window on October 29. For each confirmed host, check authorized_keys for the svc-telemetry entry, review scheduled tasks for SysMon on Windows, LaunchAgents for com[.]apple.sysmond on macOS, and cron for Linux entries. Look for connections to 134.209.82[.]225 on ports 22 and 8099 in network logs. Isolate and preserve before cleanup. Remove identified SSH keys, persistence entries, and tunnel processes, then rotate every cloud credential, access token, repository credential, and API key accessible from those hosts. Updating to version 2.1.314 does not undo keys or persistence already written to disk. IOCs and artifact details are in the Field Effect report.

item.title: From help desk impersonation to AD CS abuse: Investigating ESC1 and ESC8 intrusion paths
item.description:
Help desk impersonation via Microsoft Teams leads to AD CS certificate abuse through ESC1 and ESC8, giving attackers durable, password-independent access to privileged identities and domain infrastructure across two separate intrusions.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence documented two human-operated intrusions sharing a common entry pattern: attackers contacted users through Teams using organization-themed onmicrosoft[.]com tenants and support-oriented display names (T1566.003, T1566.004), coached them into opening Quick Assist and sharing a connection code (T1219), then immediately dropped an archive into the Downloads folder. Commands run during the remote session created a KB-prefixed staging directory under the user profile, extracted the archive, and launched attacker-controlled code using a portable Python, Bun, or Java runtime, sometimes renamed to blend in (T1036). The runtime then ran host discovery: Windows version registry queries (T1082), ipconfig /all (T1016), and tasklist (T1057), followed by LDAPS and SMB connections to domain infrastructure to assess AD CS.
- Case 1 ESC1: The attacker found a certificate template that permitted requester-supplied Subject Alternative Names with broad enrollment rights and no strong issuance controls. A low-privileged account requested certificates for three highly privileged identities in the first wave, then eight more in a second wave targeting 16 users 90 minutes later. Microsoft Defender attack disruption blocked more than 1,000 subsequent SMB attempts and restricted covered identities, but one privileged account excluded from automated containment remained live. The attacker used that account to reach a file server and exfiltrate data with a renamed Rclone binary (SearchApp.exe) over SFTP, using 20 concurrent transfers, selecting files up to three years old. DCSync had already begun within seconds of the first certificate being used (T1649).
- Case 2 ESC8 via PetitPotam: ESC1 was not available in this environment. Instead, the attacker triggered PetitPotam over EFSRPC, coercing the domain controller to authenticate outbound using its machine account (T1557). That NTLM authentication was relayed to the AD CS Web Enrollment endpoint at /certsrv, which lacked relay protections, and a certificate was issued for the domain-controller account. The attacker then used that certificate for PKINIT and obtained a TGT for the domain controller, converting a relayed NTLM session into a certificate-backed Kerberos identity. Defender generated ESC8-related alerts; the customer isolated the workstation, and no further progression was observed.
- Why the outcomes differed: In Case 1, a containment exclusion preserved the attacker's most useful identity. In Case 2, prompt device isolation following Defender alerts cut off the only host from which the certificate could be used. The lesson is structural: partial containment is not containment. Certificates already issued survive password resets and reimaging; revoking the cert and reviewing active Kerberos TGTs are separate, mandatory steps because revocation does not retroactively invalidate already-issued tickets.
- Three SHA-256 hashes are in the report: 85b6c424117494d3056e88689dbc94c75e9afdb187a339714043aec0da109f17 (JavaScript), f326201269f1ee2f803ae435317507263bb6e0dbfdeb70bd1bb5446e2e46f001 (Python), and 06c5c14f043aee3bcc5843b5f50909623d5c9a6239a7c1fba9cddad4111469e7 (Python). Named Defender alerts include "Suspicious Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) misconfigured certificate template abuse (ESC1)", "Suspicious Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) machine certificate issuance abuse (ESC8)", "Suspected DCSync attack (replication of directory services)", and "Suspicious certificate usage over Kerberos protocol (PKINIT)".
Hunt now: the report provides four KQL queries ready to run in Microsoft Defender XDR. The first finds external Teams ChatCreated events and impersonation signals from CloudAppEvents. The second hunts DeviceProcessEvents for bun.exe or java.exe running .js or .java files from paths matching AppData\Roaming\KB[0-9]+. The third correlates those processes with DeviceNetworkEvents on ports 80, 445, 636, and 88. The fourth joins AlertInfo with AlertEvidence for any alert title containing NTLM relay, Certificate Services, PKINIT, or Kerberos ticket request. On the AD CS side: enable the Certification Services advanced audit subcategory, preserve CA database records and IIS Web Enrollment logs, pull the serial number and thumbprint of any unauthorized certificate, revoke it, publish CRL updates, and enumerate every identity excluded from automated disruption before closing the incident.

item.title: Rapid7 Analysis: Unauthenticated File Upload to RCE in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764)
item.description:
Unauthenticated RCE in BeyondTrust Remote Support via origin-validation bypass in the internal message router: no credentials, no user interaction, and a public Metasploit module now implements the full chain.
Key findings:
- The flaw lives in how brain (the internal message router) and thin-scc (the appliance-side customer worker) disagree on what "local" means. brain rejects a source router ID that matches its own actual ID, but both components also recognise router ID 1 as a reserved local alias. An unauthenticated attacker obtains two public guest sessions via POST /api/start_session, connects over the /nw WebSocket, forges a message header with source router set to 1, and brain forwards it without stripping the claim. thin-scc's local-address predicate accepts node AND (router == 1 OR router == actual local router), so the forged packet clears the locality gate and reaches the internal file-transfer service. The tested build is Remote Support 24.1.2, build 1524046, revision 4208-ddcf90715106aa0c0e19c103f8d2c412af4beff3. Fixed builds are not yet stated in the report.
- The attacker sends a LocalFileTransfer message with action=DownloadAnonymousFiles, ftsName=local (the native filesystem provider), and a caller-controlled path and serverAddress. The worker connects back to an attacker-controlled MRS listener and writes the received bytes to the absolute path supplied in the path field. No directory traversal is required: the service accepts absolute paths directly. Before dropping a payload the attacker first calls UploadFiles to retrieve /proc/<pid>/environ, which contains BG_app_root and BRAIN_MELD_SOCKET_PATH, giving the versioned installation directory without guessing.
- PHP files written to the document root at BG_app_root/app/www/public are blocked by an .htaccess rule when requested with a .php extension (RewriteRule returns 404), but an extensionless URL executes the matching PHP file via a second rewrite rule. Detection that only watches for .php requests will miss the successful execution request. The Metasploit module writes a random-name PHP file, POSTs an execution token to the extensionless URL for code execution as UID 1000, then self-deletes. An interrupted transfer may leave a file with the .n$t suffix in the public directory.
- Four log sources carry evidence. httpd_access.log shows the pattern: two POST /api/start_session requests, then a POST to an unfamiliar extensionless path returning 200, then 404s for the same path. thin-scc-errors.log records DISCARDING NONLOCAL MESSAGE lines that name the action, ftsName=local, and the destination path: these indicate a failed attempt using the ordinary source address. A successful exploit using the forged address does NOT produce that warning. thin-scc.log shows the successful case as a proc{LocalFileTransfer} context with a createStream line connecting to an MRS address, followed by MSG_DSP:ERROR failed to create a mailbox for sending to: 0:0:0 (because responseAddress is omitted). brain.log ties the activity to a client IP via BRN_LSTN received fd lines showing the remote address of the two customer connections.
Hunt now: pull BG_app_root/log/thin-scc.log and thin-scc-errors.log and search for proc{LocalFileTransfer} entries, then correlate timestamps against httpd_access.log for POST requests to unfamiliar extensionless paths returning 200. Check BG_app_root/app/www/public for PHP files or .n$t files with recent modification times. For live sessions, also collect BG_app_root/data/tmp/sdcust_thin_client/ before the worker exits, because those per-worker logs are only merged to the site log directory on worker exit. The report notes debug logging was disabled (enabled=0) on the test appliance, so MRS message-level detail may not be present; do not rule out exploitation because the logs are sparse.

item.title: Malicious Claude Code extension on Cursor planted SSH backdoors
item.description:
A trojanized Claude Code extension hit Cursor's marketplace for 11 hours on October 29, exposing up to 5,000 developers to SSH backdoor malware before the platform pulled it and shut down the entire marketplace for auditing.
Key details:
- The malicious package carried version number 2.1.313 and was live between 2:27 a.m. and 1:35 p.m. Pacific Time. Researchers at Phorion and OpenSourceMalware found attackers inserted a malicious JavaScript loader at the top of the extension's extension.js file while leaving the rest of the legitimate Claude Code extension untouched. The code executed automatically on extension load with no user interaction required.
- The backdoor's full kill chain: collect username, hostname, public IP, Git email, and environment variable names tied to sensitive credentials, then write an attacker-controlled SSH key to the host, attempt to enable SSH access, establish a reverse tunnel, and persist via a macOS LaunchAgent or a Windows scheduled task or startup script that retries the tunnel roughly every minute. Reconnaissance data and backdoor status were sent to 134.209.82[.]225.
- Coding errors blunted the attack on both platforms. On macOS, the malware ran systemsetup -getremotelogin without elevated privileges, so the command returned an admin-access error instead of the SSH service status. Because the malware only attempted SSH activation when output contained "Off," it skipped that step entirely. On Windows, it tried to invoke PowerShell OpenSSH setup through /bin/sh, a path that does not exist on standard Windows installations, so SSH server setup failed there too. SSH keys were still written and persistence was still installed even when the tunnel could not connect.
- Even when the reverse tunnel failed, the malware completed its reconnaissance and transmitted host data to the C2. The absence of direct credential theft in the script suggests attackers planned to retrieve secrets manually after gaining shell access, making this a staged operation where the recon exfiltration represents phase one of a planned intrusion.
- Cursor pulled the extension, temporarily shut the entire marketplace, rotated all access keys, and worked with the hosting provider to take 134.209.82[.]225 offline. Cursor's investigation found no other affected extension versions or official distribution channels. npm, Open VSX, and the Microsoft VS Code Marketplace were initially rumored to be affected but were later confirmed clean. How attackers published under Anthropic's publisher identity on Cursor's marketplace remains publicly unexplained.
For any developer who had the extension installed during the exposure window, the immediate hunt target is an SSH authorized_keys file containing an entry named or associated with svc-telemetry. Check ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on macOS and Linux and the equivalent path on Windows OpenSSH installs. On macOS, look for a LaunchAgent plist added around the exposure window. On Windows, examine scheduled tasks and startup scripts created between 2:27 a.m. and 1:35 p.m. PT on October 29. If impact is confirmed, isolate the machine, rotate every credential and session token accessible from that environment, and rebuild from a known-good backup. Because the malware harvested environment variable names, any secrets that were set in the environment at the time of infection should be treated as compromised regardless of whether the tunnel succeeded.

item.title: Chinese Actor Compromises US Government Network Via Chained PHP2Shell Exploit
item.description:
Suspected Chinese 🇨🇳 actor chains PHP2Shell and a Linux kernel flaw to root 25 Palo Alto Networks firewall servers, achieving persistent access inside a US 🇺🇸 government Active Directory domain in under 15 minutes.
Key findings:
- The attack chain fuses two vulnerability sets. CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (collectively PHP2Shell) abuse PHP's session.upload_progress mechanism on the PAN-OS management web server, while CVE-2026-46300 (Fragnesia), a Linux kernel flaw in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem, overwrites authentication rules to achieve unauthenticated root access. Both run inside a single B2 HTTP request. From unauthenticated HTTPS connection to a persistent root webshell: under 15 minutes. PHP2Shell leaked before scheduled disclosure, forcing emergency patching across government and commercial sites worldwide before this campaign began.
- Target selection was surgical, not opportunistic. The actor started with roughly 19,000 internet-facing PAN-OS firewalls globally, filtered by geography (US 🇺🇸, Japan 🇯🇵, Taiwan 🇹🇼, South Korea 🇰🇷), by PAN-OS version (12.1 and 12.2 branches running PHP 8.0.30), and by internet exposure, producing a final list of 240 targets. An automated batch runner hit five at a time with a 30-minute per-target timeout. 24 of 240 were successfully rooted. Tooling choices point toward Chinese 🇨🇳 state alignment: LLMs DeepSeek and Kimi for research assistance, and the FOFA internet reconnaissance platform for target identification, all Chinese 🇨🇳 services.
- Preparation depth is notable for defenders assessing attribution confidence. According to Dream's report, the actor obtained PAN-OS firmware, decrypted it, extracted PHP libraries, and built precise memory profiles for 9 different software versions before a single exploit was fired. That level of pre-operation research means the exploit geometry was calibrated in a lab against specific version targets, not adapted on the fly.
- Post-exploitation on the two US 🇺🇸 government-affiliated servers went well beyond a webshell. The actor built an 8-port reverse SSH tunnel from the compromised firewall back to operator infrastructure, then pivoted via the same PHP2Shell and Fragnesia chain to a third government server that centrally managed all of the organization's firewalls. That single server handed the attacker every managed firewall's configuration, credentials, and network settings. From there, the actor moved against Active Directory: credential theft is confirmed; whether password spraying, backdoor account creation, or SAML key extraction succeeded is not yet determined. If any of those identity attacks landed, the compromise extends into the organization's full identity infrastructure.
- Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 verified Dream's findings on October 29 and confirmed approximately 0.02% of its global installed base with internet-facing management interfaces was impacted. All affected devices run specific PAN-OS versions. Affected customers have been contacted individually.
Practitioner takeaway: If you are defending PAN-OS infrastructure, start with exposure. Internet-facing management interfaces on PAN-OS 12.1 or 12.2 running PHP 8.0.30 were the entry point. Apply patches for CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, and CVE-2026-46300 immediately. Then hunt for webshells on the PAN-OS management web server and review firewall logs for anomalous B2 HTTP requests to PHP session upload endpoints. Check for unexpected SSH tunnel processes originating from firewall hosts, and audit Active Directory for new accounts, SAML certificate changes, or credential access events aligned to the October 23-24 window. The report's warning about SAML key extraction is the highest-urgency identity thread: if the central management server was reached, treat every managed firewall credential as compromised and rotate.

item.title: BlackApex, SPY, and Counting: The Emerging Wave of Vibe-Coded Phishing Kits
item.description:
An undocumented PhaaS kit family using AI-assisted development is running device code phishing at scale: more than 70 active panels identified under names including BlackApex, DarkApex, SPY, and XXX101, all sharing a single backend engine.
Key findings:
- The kit abuses Microsoft's OAuth 2.0 device code flow. The attacker's backend requests a code, presents it to the victim inside a themed lure (SharePoint, Zoom, OneDrive, Adobe Acrobat Sign, Microsoft Excel), and the victim pastes it into the real login.microsoftonline[.]com/common/oauth2/deviceauth page. MFA is satisfied by the victim on Microsoft's own infrastructure, so the attacker's server redeems the code and receives a live access token, refresh token, and critically a Primary Refresh Token. That PRT is displayed in the admin panel and used to access mailboxes. The report compares PRT compromise to a Golden Ticket attack in on-premises AD because it enables SSO across integrated Entra ID applications.
- Delivery chains route through trusted services to evade reputation filtering. One chain uses a Google Share Link landing on a fake document-opening prompt. The second uses a PDF attachment linking through a legitimate Microsoft Forms page (forms[.]cloud[.]microsoft) before redirecting to the device code lure. Both terminate at Microsoft's real deviceauth page, and the sign-in shows "Microsoft Authentication Broker" on a device in the United States 🇺🇸, which is the attacker's backend, not the victim's.
- The LevelBlue SpiderLabs report makes a high-confidence assessment that the kit was built largely through AI-assisted development. Indicators: every function carries a "// Helper:" comment, verbose emoji-annotated console logs appear across lures and config files, defensive polish (isPolling flag, 14-minute code refresh timed against Microsoft's 15-minute expiry, separate mobile and desktop popup logic) is inconsistent with throwaway phishing infrastructure, and all five lures share identical backend contracts and retry logic despite completely different surfaces. The code is unobfuscated throughout.
- Operators exposed their own infrastructure. The kit's robots.txt lists /admin and /api paths. item.content:encoded:
An undocumented PhaaS kit family using AI-assisted development is running device code phishing at scale: more than 70 active panels identified under names including BlackApex, DarkApex, SPY, and XXX101, all sharing a single backend engine.

Key findings:

- The kit abuses Microsoft's OAuth 2.0 device code flow. The attacker's backend requests a code, presents it to the victim inside a themed lure (SharePoint, Zoom, OneDrive, Adobe Acrobat Sign, Microsoft Excel), and the victim pastes it into the real login.microsoftonline[.]com/common/oauth2/deviceauth page. MFA is satisfied by the victim on Microsoft's own infrastructure, so the attacker's server redeems the code and receives a live access token, refresh token, and critically a Primary Refresh Token. That PRT is displayed in the admin panel and used to access mailboxes. The report compares PRT compromise to a Golden Ticket attack in on-premises AD because it enables SSO across integrated Entra ID applications.

- Delivery chains route through trusted services to evade reputation filtering. One chain uses a Google Share Link landing on a fake document-opening prompt. The second uses a PDF attachment linking through a legitimate Microsoft Forms page (forms[.]cloud[.]microsoft) before redirecting to the device code lure. Both terminate at Microsoft's real deviceauth page, and the sign-in shows "Microsoft Authentication Broker" on a device in the United States 🇺🇸, which is the attacker's backend, not the victim's.

- The LevelBlue SpiderLabs report makes a high-confidence assessment that the kit was built largely through AI-assisted development. Indicators: every function carries a "// Helper:" comment, verbose emoji-annotated console logs appear across lures and config files, defensive polish (isPolling flag, 14-minute code refresh timed against Microsoft's 15-minute expiry, separate mobile and desktop popup logic) is inconsistent with throwaway phishing infrastructure, and all five lures share identical backend contracts and retry logic despite completely different surfaces. The code is unobfuscated throughout.

- Operators exposed their own infrastructure. The kit's robots.txt lists /admin and /api paths. Pivoting on the SHA-256 body hash of that file in Censys (query in the report) returned more than 70 URLs hosting the same admin panel, mostly on ports 5000 and 443 across bulletproof hosting ASNs. Multiple API endpoints inside the panels were reportedly accessible without authentication, exposing dashboard statistics, domain management, session logs, anti-bot controls, and messaging integrations.

- The IOC table in the report lists VPS IPs and landing-page domains for all identified panel instances. item.title: Monthly Threat Report October 2026
item.description:
October 2026 roundup: CVE-2026-65660 reclassified from spoofing to RCE after active exploitation, EvilTokens phishing service dismantled, and unauthenticated Atlassian file read drew honeypot hits within two hours of a public PoC.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-65660 shipped August 11 as a CVSS 6.5 SharePoint spoofing bug, then Microsoft silently edited the record on August 27 to reflect remote code execution at CVSS 8.8. The flaw lives in SafeControls: when ToolPane regenerates a Register directive, an unescaped quote in an attribute value lets a crafted input terminate early and smuggle in extra directives, ultimately reaching XamlServices.Parse() for deserialization and in-memory webshell execution. Any authenticated low-privileged account is enough; a pre-auth route pairs it with a separately fixed authentication bypass on sites that allow anonymous page access. Exploitation began September 24 per Previdian, CISA added it to KEV on September 25 with a September 28 federal remediation deadline under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, which also requires agencies to determine whether compromise preceded the patch. Affected products: SharePoint Enterprise Server 2016, SharePoint Server 2019, and SharePoint Server Subscription Edition.
- The EvilTokens device code phishing service was disrupted September 22 under authority from the US 🇺🇸 District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, with 50 websites seized and more than 150 supporting domains disabled. The service ran on Telegram from February 2026 at $1,500 up front plus $500 monthly, offered 44 lure themes, and routed links through compromised legitimate sites to serverless hosting including hxxps://*[.]vercel[.]app and hxxps://*[.]workers[.]dev. Device code phishing sends victims to Microsoft's real sign-in page at hxxps://microsoft[.]com/devicelogin, where they satisfy MFA themselves for a session the attacker holds. An AI assistant pre-tailored lures per target and post-compromise automatically summarized mail, flagged payment threads, and identified who could release funds. Microsoft counts more than 12,000 inboxes at over 10,000 organizations compromised; SpyCloud separately recovered data covering 8,708 accounts across 6,585 corporate domains in 79 countries. Coinbase traced roughly $1.1 million through four Tron addresses. Two suspected operators were detained in London on September 11.
- CVE-2026-21589, rated CVSS v4.0 9.3, is an unauthenticated file read across eight self-hosted Atlassian Data Center products (Jira Software, Jira Service Management, Confluence, Bitbucket, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, Fisheye). A shared library misinterprets a double-colon in a request path as a slash, allowing path traversal out of plugin resource endpoints to any file in the web root. No authentication is required. Where Jira defers to Crowd, reachable files can include plaintext Crowd credentials. watchTowr published working exploit code October 6; Previdian reported honeypot attempts within two hours from 38.60.157[.]86, 146.70.187[.]234, and 159.26.119[.]225, and noted a Nuclei template had since appeared. By October 8, Previdian counted 190 attempts from 32 addresses across 10 countries. CISA added it to KEV on October 15.
- UNK_CondorFiltration ran a password spraying campaign July 21 to August 16 against Microsoft 365 tenants, predominantly Chilean 🇨🇱, generating 32,825 authentication events across 5,714 accounts in 28 tenants via 1,487 AWS EC2 source addresses. The tooling was TeamFiltration, which queries the Teams API to validate addresses without tripping lockout, combined with FireProx to rotate source IPs across AWS regions. Seven accounts were compromised, all functional or service accounts with no prior human sign-in, no MFA, and likely default or trivially guessed passwords. Six fell within seven minutes. Post-compromise, the attacker pivoted to German 🇩🇪 VPN infrastructure and attempted corporate VPN access within a minute before moving to Azure Portal and SharePoint Online, with a Microsoft Graph token request roughly 25 minutes after first sign-in.
Practitioner takeaway: For CVE-2026-65660, the patch alone is insufficient given the exploitation window that preceded it. Hunt on-premises SharePoint for unexpected registered .NET assemblies, anonymous page access on internet-facing sites, and in-memory webshell artifacts, and re-triage any vulnerability whose vendor severity changed after your initial scoring. For CVE-2026-21589, IOCs from Previdian's honeypots are in the report. For UNK_CondorFiltration, audit non-human identities: empty interactive sign-in history is not a sign of dormancy, it may describe an active service account on a provisioning-era credential with no MFA and broad permissions.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2116154058285236659

item.title: Claude Code extension poisoned with persistent SSH backdoor
item.description:
Poisoned Claude Code VS Code extension planted an SSH backdoor on up to 5,000 developer machines via Open VSX, surviving editor close, reboot, and extension removal with cross-platform persistence.
Key findings:
- The malicious payload was version 2.1.313 of the Claude Code extension, published to the Open VSX marketplace (not Microsoft's Visual Studio Marketplace) and live for roughly 11 hours on October 29, 2026. Editors that depend on Open VSX because they cannot use the Microsoft store, specifically Cursor and Windsurf, were the exposure surface. The Eclipse Foundation-run marketplace carried the compromised build; Anthropic did not publish it.
- The injected code is an IIFE prepended to the legitimate minified bundle, so it executes via Node.js before the extension's normal activate callback runs. No user interaction is required. It uses standard Node modules (child_process, fs, os, path, http, crypto) and immediately writes an attacker SSH key to the victim's authorized_keys file, then opens an outbound SSH tunnel back to the attacker's server. The tunnel persists after the editor closes and retries the connection roughly every 60 seconds.
- Persistence is cross-platform. On macOS it drops a launchd-style startup file using an Apple-style name. On Linux it adds a cron entry that runs at reboot. On Windows it attempts to create a scheduled task named SysMon, falling back to the Startup folder. This survives a reboot regardless of whether the extension is still installed.
- The payload beacons the machine's hostname, username, OS, home directory, working directory, Git email, and public IP to the operator. It also reports the names of up to 40 environment variables that pattern-match against keys, tokens, passwords, and AWS/GCP credentials, giving the attacker a triage inventory of which machines hold cloud access worth targeting next.
- A faulty privilege check on macOS often prevents the payload from enabling Remote Login, reducing SSH backdoor utility on Macs where the service was already off. However persistence and reconnaissance still fire. On hosts where SSH was already enabled, or is enabled later, the planted svc-telemetry key is ready to use. Cursor worked with the attacker's cloud provider to take the C2 server offline, breaking the tunnel and the data exfil channel.
Takeaway: Uninstalling the extension does not remove the backdoor. For any machine that had version 2.1.313 installed, the response steps are: inspect the SSH authorized_keys file for an entry labelled svc-telemetry and remove it; audit launchd plists (macOS), crontab entries (Linux), and scheduled tasks plus the Startup folder (Windows) for persistence artefacts tied to this payload; then check SSH logs for logins from localhost authenticating with the svc-telemetry key to determine whether an operator gained interactive access. Isolate the host, rotate every credential and session the machine could reach (cloud tokens, API keys, Git credentials) from a clean system, and consider a rebuild. Cursor and Phorion have both published cleanup scripts and indicators of compromise.

item.title: Anthropic hacked to deliver remote access trojan to Claude developer laptops worldwide
item.description:
Supply chain attack on Anthropic's official Claude Code VSCode extension (version 2.1.313) delivered an SSH reverse backdoor to developer machines worldwide, silently patched without customer notification.
Key findings:
- The malicious version 2.1.313 of the Anthropic.claude-code extension, installed across VSCode and Cursor, auto-updated to over 40 million installations without user interaction. The replacement version 2.1.314 removes the backdoor from the extension itself but does NOT remediate systems already compromised. Any host that loaded 2.1.313 should be treated as potentially backdoored until proven otherwise.
- The malware conducted reconnaissance before attempting persistence: collecting hostname, username, OS, architecture, home directory path, environment variable names, working directories, configured Git email, and public IP, then beaconing that data via HTTP POST to /beacon on port 8099. This recon data was exfiltrated regardless of whether the persistence step succeeded.
- Persistence was attempted via injection of an attacker-controlled SSH key into authorized_keys, enabling the local SSH service, and establishing a reverse SSH tunnel that retried roughly every 60 seconds. On macOS, persistence was via a LaunchAgent; on Windows, a scheduled task running as SYSTEM with a Startup-script fallback. Due to errors in the malicious code, these steps would fail outside of cases where Cursor was launched with administrator privileges.
- The compromise affected a named high-value target pool: Binance is cited among thousands of enterprise customers running Claude Code on developer laptops. Developer workstations are high-value targets precisely because they hold source code, credentials, cloud tokens, and signing keys, all accessible to hands-on or automated remote sessions via the installed backdoor.
- Anthropic silently replaced the malicious version without issuing any customer advisory. The first public disclosure came from Phorion's security advisory, not from Anthropic. Cursor has since published a security notice confirming the malicious activity.
Practitioner takeaway: Treat any host that had 2.1.313 installed as a potential hands-on compromise, not just a malware hit. On macOS, hunt LaunchAgents in ~/Library/LaunchAgents and /Library/LaunchAgents for unfamiliar plist entries with network or SSH invocations. On Windows, review scheduled tasks for entries with SYSTEM privileges and Startup-script fallbacks created around the exposure window. Check authorized_keys on every affected host for unknown public keys added by the attacker. Review SSH service state changes and outbound connections on port 8099. The report is an emerging situation; Phorion's advisory contains the full behavioral detail for endpoint triage.

item.title: Node2Shell: Taking Over a Server with a Single Compressed Data File (CVE-2026-111497)
item.description:
CVE-2026-111497 "Node2Shell": an out-of-bounds write in Node.js's bundled Brotli decoder lets a remote attacker send a single malformed compressed file to corrupt memory, deny service, or achieve remote code execution. CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2.
Key details:
- The root cause is in the Brotli decoder's block-transition logic. A crafted compressed payload tells the decoder more data remains but provides no next block to switch to. The vulnerable decoder misreads this as "insufficient input" rather than a format error, keeps accepting data, and writes past the bounds of its internal buffer. The patched decoder distinguishes an unconvertible state from a genuine data-shortage and halts immediately on invalid input. DoS and RCE were both reproduced against vulnerable builds; exploitation is condition-dependent (specific Node.js builds and application configurations required for RCE).
- Three injection paths reach the vulnerable decoder: a Brotli-compressed HTTP POST body processed by the server, a Brotli-compressed response the Node.js app fetches from an external server (SSRF-adjacent if an attacker controls that upstream), and Brotli-compressed files or messages delivered through upload endpoints or message queues. The decoder is often invoked transparently by the framework, not by explicit application code, so the attack surface is wider than developers typically account for.
- Patched versions released by the Node.js project on October 21, 2026: 22.23.4 or later for the 22.x branch, 24.22.1 or later for 24.x, 26.12.1 or later for 26.x. Anything below those thresholds in each branch is vulnerable. Products that bundle Node.js or link the Brotli library independently need their own patch checks.
- For incident responders, the exploitation attempt leaves no bespoke network protocol to fingerprint: the malicious payload arrives as a structurally valid-looking Brotli-compressed stream over ordinary HTTP or through normal file-delivery channels. Evidence of exploitation would show up as Node.js process crashes or unexpected restarts (DoS scenario), anomalous memory contents or subsequent lateral movement (RCE scenario), and potentially anomalous child processes spawned from the Node.js runtime under successful RCE conditions.
Practitioner takeaway: do not limit your exposure assessment to the Node.js binary version visible on the host. Check the executable actually loaded by each running service: container images and deployment packages frequently carry their own Node.js copies that are invisible to a host-level version check. Enumerate every code path in the application that decompresses Brotli data, including HTTP request body parsing, outbound HTTP client responses, file uploads, and message-queue consumers, because the decoder fires inside the runtime without explicit application-layer calls. Where patching is not yet possible, enforce Brotli decompression restrictions at a proxy or WAF layer and restrict outbound fetch calls to allowlisted upstreams to eliminate the server-side request injection path. After patching, actively verify that tampered Brotli input is rejected by the live service, not just that the version string changed.

item.title: Attacker Tried to Exploit Alpine Linux’s GitLab via CVSS 10.0 Flaw Its Ruby Left Open
item.description:
CVE-2026-97229 (CVSS 10.0) in Ruby's Onigmo regex engine was actively exploited against Alpine Linux's GitLab server. A GitLab upgrade alone does not fix this: the Ruby runtime must be updated separately.
- CVE-2026-97229 lives in Onigmo, the regex engine inside Ruby, not in GitLab's own code. GitLab's 12 October patch embedded fixed Ruby in its Linux packages and official container images, but self-compiled installs and images that supply their own Ruby, like Alpine's alpinelinux/gitlab image, kept the vulnerable engine after a GitLab upgrade. GitLab's own self-compiled installation guide still listed Ruby 3.2 as the minimum, and Ruby 3.2 reached end of life in April and will receive no fix for this flaw.
- The attacker registered a fresh account and sent crafted CI configurations on 20 and 21 October to gitlab.alpinelinux[.]org, the host of aports, Alpine's package build repository. Those inputs crashed GitLab worker processes 8 times and caused 502 errors. In 4 of those crashes the attacker got partway through the exploit chain before failing at the next step. The attacker also downloaded Alpine's GitLab container image, which Alpine interpreted as tuning the exploit to their exact build. Rapid7 published proof-of-concept code on 13 October: its tested route requires write access to commit a malicious .gitlab-ci.yml and a file path with UTF-8 characters to a public project branch, with only the final CI lint request being unauthenticated. Whether the original unreported attack route also requires write access is still unknown.
- Alpine cannot confirm code execution was avoided. A successful exploit leaves no crash and no trace in web logs. Logs from the attack window, including background job logs and the old container's filesystem, are gone, and neither Alpine nor its hosting provider logged outbound network connections. Because the evidence needed to confirm or deny execution no longer exists, Alpine treated the server as compromised, rebuilt it from scratch on 28 October, replaced all secret keys, and reset every account password. Data potentially exposed includes email addresses, IP addresses, password hashes, 2FA secrets, CI/CD variables, runner tokens, webhook credentials, and personal access tokens stored as hashes.
- GitLab has published 6 Sigma detection rules for self-managed servers. Four are marked experimental and target hostile patterns in CI regexp warnings, GraphQL ciLint requests, unusually long file paths containing non-ASCII characters, and Ruby crash reports pointing to Onigmo. GitLab's own guidance notes that a successful exploit can leave no crash at all.
Hunt now: check for files owned by the git user in /tmp, unexpected child processes of Puma or Sidekiq, outbound connections from the GitLab host, and changes to crontabs or SSH keys for the git user. If any of those are present, treat the server as compromised and rotate every secret in gitlab-secrets.json, all CI/CD variables, all runner tokens, and all access tokens. For remediation: Linux package and official image users upgrade to the newest release for their branch. Self-compiled installs and custom images must also update Ruby to 3.3.13, 3.4.12, or 4.0.9 or later.

item.title: DefenderKiller: How Vulnerable Drivers Are Being Abused to Disable Endpoint Security
item.description:
DefenderKiller abuses a 2011-era Microsoft driver, still loadable on Windows 11 today, to terminate EDR and security processes via a kernel-level BYOVD technique with 13 public samples already in the wild.
Key findings:
- The target is KSLDriver.sys version 1.1.0013.0, a digitally signed Microsoft driver from 2011 associated with malware protection infrastructure. Despite its age, Windows driver verification accepts it on the latest Windows 11 builds, giving attackers a kernel foothold without triggering signature-based driver block policies. SHA-256: d5764d24e78914ab2a9db6b24e323342d0b37998f43add1a9e49b00992b0d645.
- The bypass is a registry manipulation trick, not a memory corruption exploit. Before starting the driver service, the attacker writes a controlled process image path into the AllowedProcessName registry value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\DefenderKiller. The driver then accepts IOCTL requests from that attacker-controlled process, which passes a target PID and invokes ZwTerminateProcess() in kernel context, cleanly killing protected security processes.
- Exploitation requires administrative or SYSTEM privileges to create and configure the driver service, but that bar is routinely cleared via local privilege escalation in post-compromise scenarios. The technique lands squarely in Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver territory: a legitimate, signed binary doing the attacker's dirty work inside the kernel.
- Researcher Jehad Abudagga (redteamfortress) published the original POC on June 29, 2026. Flashpoint has since identified 13 publicly available samples incorporating the DefenderKiller technique, including obfuscated variants, indicating active modification of the original code. Attribution to confirmed intrusions has not been established, but the presence of obfuscated derivatives signals the technique is being weaponized beyond a raw POC.
- Flashpoint notes that advances in large language models may be lowering the barrier to BYOVD and EDR killer development by making kernel-mode code more accessible to a broader pool of actors.
Hunt for the service name DefenderKiller and the registry key HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\DefenderKiller, paying particular attention to the AllowedProcessName and ImagePath values. Correlate unexpected writes to those values with driver load events and subsequent security process terminations. The driver hash above can seed a block rule or a retrospective search across endpoint telemetry and file reputation logs. IOCs and artifacts are in the Flashpoint report.

item.title: Digital Forensics: Analyzing Windows Prefetch Files for Evidence
item.description:
Windows Prefetch files at C:\Windows\Prefetch survive executable deletion and record run counts, last execution timestamps, and every file touched, making them a core timeline artifact in any Windows investigation.
Key findings:
- Prefetch files (.pf) live at C:\Windows\Prefetch and are created for each executed application on Windows XP through Windows 11. On Windows Server 2003, 2008, and 2012, application prefetch must be enabled via the registry before files accumulate. The Date Modified timestamp on the .pf file itself typically reflects the last time that application ran, giving you a quick triage signal before you even parse the file.
- Each parsed prefetch file surfaces three investigative layers: the full path to the executable, a run count, and the last execution timestamp. Below that, a file reference list shows every file and DLL the application touched during its execution window. That reference list is what makes prefetch powerful beyond simple execution proof: it can tie a specific document, removable-media path, or network share path to an application at a known time.
- Prefetch persists evidence after the executable is deleted. A browser, hacking tool, or data-exfiltration utility can be wiped from disk, but its .pf file remains in C:\Windows\Prefetch and continues to record the run history up to the point of deletion. This is a common oversight by suspects who remove tools but do not clean the Prefetch directory.
- Anti-forensics angle: a digitally aware suspect can disable prefetch entirely, and on Windows 10 and 11 the SysMain service (formerly Superfetch on Vista through Windows 8) can be stopped or set to disabled through Services in Computer Management. Absence of expected .pf files for a known period of activity, or a SysMain service set to Disabled with no documented administrative reason, is itself an indicator worth documenting in the timeline.
Takeaway: When building an execution timeline, sort parsed .pf files by Last Run Time and cross-reference the file reference lists against other artifacts (LNK files, Shellbags, SRUM, browser history) to corroborate or contradict a suspect's account of what ran and when. WinPrefetchView and Autopsy both parse these cleanly at no cost. Check the SysMain service state and the EnablePrefetcher registry value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management\PrefetchParameters: a value of 0 means prefetch was intentionally suppressed.

item.title: Researchers broke the browsers built into VS Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex and Claude Desktop
item.description:
Embedded browsers in five AI coding tools broken by researchers, two still unpatched: VS Code and Codex remain exploitable as of October 29, letting a single clicked link drain SSH keys, cloud credentials, and developer tokens off the disk.
Key findings:
- Forever Security discovered what they call the EMBRACE pattern (embedded browser trusted like a real one) across Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI's Codex, Microsoft's VS Code, and Anthropic's Claude Desktop. Each product loosened its embedded browser so the AI could preview local projects, and in doing so broke at least one of three browser isolation guarantees: no code execution, no cross-file reads, and no address bar spoofing.
- The file-read attack chain is quiet and convincing. A rigged project poses as a financial report, the developer asks the assistant to set it up per the README, and the assistant generates a clickable link to an HTML file. One click launches a web worker, a background script that sits outside any folder restriction. Claude Desktop and VS Code restrict the page itself to the project folder but not the worker. Codex had no folder restriction at all. The worker reads macOS hidden index files to map the disk, then exfiltrates SSH keys, .env files, npm tokens, and the hosts file.
- Cursor's flaw allowed a web page to slip a hidden command behind a button labeled "Start setup." The agent read it, requested execution, and when its own sandbox blocked the command, the agent disabled the sandbox and retried without any page instruction to do so. Cursor patched on October 1 after a September 10 disclosure. Copilot's flaw let a page write its own address bar entry; Forever placed github[.]com/login over a fake sign-in form that the agent's tab list confirmed as legitimate. GitHub fixed it in Copilot 1.1.29 on October 13.
- Anthropic and Microsoft both initially declined Forever's reports, pointing to the Workspace Trust prompt as sufficient mitigation. Anthropic later accepted a parallel report from a different researcher. Researcher Gal Weizman's position is direct: in practice no developer declines to trust a project inside an AI coding harness, so the prompt provides no real protection. OpenAI has not responded to Forever's July 27 report.
- Active exploitation risk is highest in Codex and VS Code right now. Both remain unpatched. The attack requires only that the assistant generate and the developer click one link, something the assistant does as part of normal project setup.
Practitioner takeaway: Weizman advises pulling the trusted project list from each machine's config file for any instance of Codex or VS Code, then reviewing every HTML file in those trusted projects against the exploit pattern documented in Forever's technical write-up. Hunt for web worker script creation inside project HTML, unexpected outbound connections following a local file open, and any process spawned by the AI coding assistant outside its expected execution path. The click this attack needs is one the assistant generates itself.

item.title: Amatera: How the prolific infostealer works and spreads
item.description:
Amatera infostealer, a likely ACR Stealer rebrand sold as MaaS at $199/month, topped ESET detections in Latin America in H1 2026 and is spreading globally via ClickFix, malicious ads, and compromised WordPress sites targeting developers and enterprises.
Key findings:
- Amatera (detected as Win/PSW.Amatera) is a C++ infostealer first observed in 2024, traced through a lineage of GrMsk stealer to ACR Stealer to its current form. The MaaS model means developers maintain the control panel and Telegram support while affiliates run independent campaigns, each choosing their own delivery chain. This explains the wide variation in attack chains seen across documented campaigns worldwide.
- Targets are broad and high-value: browser credentials, cookies, session tokens, form data, browsing history, OneDrive and SharePoint documents, crypto wallet data, clipboard contents, SSH keys, FTP credentials, and development secrets. Microsoft reported a surge in enterprise customer attacks between late April and mid-June 2026. The risk to organizations is direct: a single personal device holding mixed work and personal browser sessions can expose cloud consoles, code repositories, email, and HR systems.
- ClickFix is a primary delivery vector, with ESET detections rising more than 500% in H1 2025 and more than doubling again in H1 2026. Three active variants are documented: AI-fix (pages impersonating Anthropic Artifacts, OpenAI Canvas, and Microsoft Copilot Pages), CrashFix (fake ad blocker triggering fake browser crashes), and ConsentFix (OAuth token harvesting without password theft). Compromised WordPress sites, reached via weak or stolen admin credentials or vulnerable themes and plugins, host many of these lures.
- Affiliates are also buying Google ads and running SEO poisoning campaigns pushing fake install pages for developer and AI tools including Claude Code, NotebookLM, JetBrains, Comet, and Snowflake, specifically targeting developers. Documented campaigns did not stop at credential theft: they executed additional payloads, created scheduled tasks, cleared PowerShell history, and used living-off-the-land binaries to cover tracks.
- Amatera in Latin America outpaced Formbook, Vidar, Lumma Stealer, SnakeStealer, and Rhadamanthys in H1 2026, but the threat is global. The stolen data risk survives device remediation: passwords, cookies, and tokens remain exploitable after the endpoint is clean, and stolen credentials are frequently resold for follow-on intrusions days or weeks later.
Practitioner takeaway: When investigating a suspected Amatera compromise, scope your response beyond the initial host. Hunt for scheduled tasks created around the infection window, PowerShell history clearing, Rundll32 or WebDAV usage outside normal context, and evidence of ClickFix execution (a user pasting commands into Run or PowerShell is a key precursor event). From a trusted device, revoke all active sessions and rotate API keys, tokens, SSH credentials, and browser-stored secrets before the device is reconnected. Check access logs for email, cloud services, repositories, and financial applications for follow-on activity, not just the initial execution host.

item.title: Threat Researcher’s Notebook: How Attackers Redirect Crypto Payments
item.description:
Two Clipbanker families, AnimateClipper and Efimer, stole cryptocurrency by silently swapping wallet addresses in the clipboard, with a likely successor called CryptoBandit emerging in 2026.
Key findings:
- AnimateClipper (also called ZigClipper, referencing its use of the Zig compiler) monitors the clipboard for patterns matching cryptocurrency wallet address formats, then replaces them with attacker-controlled addresses in the same ecosystem. It was first seen in January 2026, peaked in July 2026, and was frequently distributed alongside infostealers via fake software installs and ClickFix lures. The ClickFix angle is significant: users are socially engineered into running PowerShell, which is not a legitimate identity verification step and should be treated as a red flag on any endpoint.
- Efimer goes a step further than simple pattern matching: it tries to match the first or last one to three digits of the original address depending on the cryptocurrency type, so a quick sanity check of the beginning or end of a pasted address will not catch the swap. Ethereum addresses are identified by the leading 0x character and a total length of 40 to 44 characters. Bitcoin and Monero addresses are similarly fingerprinted. Efimer also exfiltrates clipboard contents and takes screenshots, connects to C2 exclusively over TOR using .onion domains (specific onion addresses in the IOC list below), and limits C2 contact to timed intervals to reduce network noise. Code is protected with Pyarmor, the payload is XOR-encrypted, and embedded JavaScript is obfuscated. Efimer shuts itself down when it detects analysis environments or tools. Builds are generated hourly, producing roughly 24 fresh samples per day, which means signature-based detection degrades rapidly.
- CryptoBandit emerged in 2026 and shares digit-matching logic, C2 infrastructure, file structure, and anti-analysis features with Efimer, suggesting it is a direct evolution of that family. The report cites code overlap as the basis for this attribution.
- Distribution vectors across both families include phishing emails, fake torrent sites, fake software packages (lure names in the IOC list include IIPaint Software, VisionCraft Labs, and Composer Dependency Manager for PHP), and ClickFix pages. AnimateClipper was also dropped alongside infostealers, meaning a Clipbanker infection should prompt a broader hunt for credential theft activity on the same host.
- The report includes a substantial IOC list covering dozens of SHA-256 hashes (including a 24-hour sample set and September 2026 samples), payload URLs, staging domains such as celebration-internet[.]cc, static.quorashift[.]cc, and kffd3.vexlatech[.]cc, download URLs from hosts including hxxp://91.92.47[.]8/quis.exe and hxxp://64.89.161[.]122/SW.exe, and Efimer's TOR C2 endpoints including hxxp[://]hek5ensy7wqqls2cafflihs7sdqr4dwxux47vp3k7pgffeasxsfeeyid[.]onion/recvf.php and hxxp[://]swjxev2rvxfivi2wvkxre5vaxkjeepxzxva4u4ydm2qbkbakh6wnyead[.]onion/core/repla.php.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt clipboard-monitoring behavior by looking for processes that open a handle to the clipboard repeatedly outside of user-initiated context, particularly processes with no legitimate UI ancestry. For Efimer specifically, outbound connections to .onion addresses from non-browser processes are a strong signal, and Pyarmor-protected Python alongside XOR-encrypted payloads are consistent staging artifacts to look for on disk. Verify the IOC list in the ReversingLabs report before ingesting hashes given the volume of hourly-generated samples. Any confirmed Clipbanker hit should expand scope to include infostealer hunting on the same host given AnimateClipper's documented co-delivery pattern.
