Efimer also exfiltrates clipboard contents and takes screenshots, connects to C2 exclusively over TOR using .onion domains (specific onion addresses in the IOC list below), and limits C2 contact to timed intervals to reduce network noise. Code is protected with Pyarmor, the payload is XOR-encrypted, and embedded JavaScript is obfuscated. Efimer shuts itself down when it detects analysis environments or tools. Builds are generated hourly, producing roughly 24 fresh samples per day, which means signature-based detection degrades rapidly.

- CryptoBandit emerged in 2026 and shares digit-matching logic, C2 infrastructure, file structure, and anti-analysis features with Efimer, suggesting it is a direct evolution of that family. The report cites code overlap as the basis for this attribution.

- Distribution vectors across both families include phishing emails, fake torrent sites, fake software packages (lure names in the IOC list include IIPaint Software, VisionCraft Labs, and Composer Dependency Manager for PHP), and ClickFix pages. AnimateClipper was also dropped alongside infostealers, meaning a Clipbanker infection should prompt a broader hunt for credential theft activity on the same host.

- The report includes a substantial IOC list covering dozens of SHA-256 hashes (including a 24-hour sample set and September 2026 samples), payload URLs, staging domains such as celebration-internet[.]cc, static.quorashift[.]cc, and kffd3.vexlatech[.]cc, download URLs from hosts including hxxp://91.92.47[.]8/quis.exe and hxxp://64.89.161[.]122/SW.exe, and Efimer's TOR C2 endpoints including hxxp[://]hek5ensy7wqqls2cafflihs7sdqr4dwxux47vp3k7pgffeasxsfeeyid[.]onion/recvf.php and hxxp[://]swjxev2rvxfivi2wvkxre5vaxkjeepxzxva4u4ydm2qbkbakh6wnyead[.]onion/core/repla.php.

Practitioner takeaway: Hunt clipboard-monitoring behavior by looking for processes that open a handle to the clipboard repeatedly outside of user-initiated context, particularly processes with no legitimate UI ancestry. For Efimer specifically, outbound connections to .onion addresses from non-browser processes are a strong signal, and Pyarmor-protected Python alongside XOR-encrypted payloads are consistent staging artifacts to look for on disk. Verify the IOC list in the ReversingLabs report before ingesting hashes given the volume of hourly-generated samples. Any confirmed Clipbanker hit should expand scope to include infostealer hunting on the same host given AnimateClipper's documented co-delivery pattern.

item.title: php2shell one week later: Why one exploit doesn’t work everywhere
item.description:
CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (php2shell, CVSSv4 9.2 each) are confirmed exploited in the wild, but mass exploitation at Log4Shell scale is not materializing: the exploit must be tuned to each target's specific PHP build, SAPI, and memory layout.
Key details:
- Both CVEs are in CISA's KEV catalog. CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw; CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free caused by stale state shared between requests on the same worker. Confirmed exploitation includes 35 shell executions on honeypots running PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php with a single worker, and a chained attack combining php2shell with Linux kernel LPE Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300, also in KEV) that reportedly rooted 25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States 🇺🇸, Japan 🇯🇵, Taiwan 🇹🇼, and South Korea 🇰🇷. Palo Alto Networks independently verified the attacker's tooling and confirmed results. By October 29, active exploitation targeting internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces was confirmed.
- Tenable's working RCE on PHP 7.4.33 required GDB-measured heap geometry specific to that exact build. Chunk-relative offsets for a PHP 8.3.35 docker-library bookworm amd64 build placed _zend_array at chunk+0x572a0 and arData at chunk+0x64b80. A Debian-packaged PHP 8.3.35, or the same version built with different extensions, produces different values. The UAF also requires worker reuse across consecutive requests: under mod_php this means keep-alive; under PHP-FPM it requires session affinity via PHPSESSID. A pm.max_requests setting that recycles workers silently breaks the entire exploitation chain.
- Tenable identified two detection signals. Signal 1: a large filename in a multipart POST produces a measurably different allocation size on vulnerable vs. patched PHP because the patched allocator rounds to a corrected size class. Signal 2: compact amplification sequences expose the UAF window via a session upload-progress oracle that watches for a crash/recover pattern under controlled amplification. Both signals together form a stateful probe but carry false-negative and false-positive risk because memory limits controlled by memory_limit, ini_set, PHP_VALUE, or PHP_ADMIN_VALUE per-request directives affect whether the OOM condition fires at all.
- The network appliance exception is the critical prioritization point. Where many devices share one PHP build, calibration cost is paid once and that single exploit reaches every device in the fleet. Roughly 30.3 million PHP services remained on affected versions as of October 29 per Censys tracking, though version match does not equal exploitability. AI-assisted tooling accelerated exploit research on both the attacker and defender side, and Tenable cautions that a successful shell is not proof a specific CVE was used: one AI agent in their lab produced a working shell via a local file inclusion weakness unrelated to php2shell.
Practitioner takeaway: prioritize internet-exposed PAN-OS and other network appliance management interfaces for immediate patching or isolation since one calibrated exploit reaches the entire fleet. For the broader PHP estate, patch to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 on your critical schedule. Hunt for the multipart POST allocation-size anomaly Tenable describes as signal 1, watch for PHPSESSID-pinned request sequences preceding worker crashes as a UAF indicator, and treat CVE-2026-46300 (Fragnesia) as part of the same incident scope given confirmed chaining.

item.title: The Ultra Trail: From Viewer to Mailer
item.description:
A DNS pivot from UltraViewer, a remote-access tool seen in tech-support scams, unraveled a QuickBooks phishing operation using 350+ lookalike domains, a bulk-mail tracking service with no abuse mechanism, and trojanized installers dropping njRAT and DarkKometa.
Key findings:
- The QuickBooks phishing campaign uses over 350 lookalike domains, the majority registered with Dynadot in a single week between June 29 and July 5, 2026. Victims receive emails urging them to call scammer numbers, including +1 (805) 835-8090 and +1 (805) 699-1139. Every email contains a 1x1 tracking pixel firing a GET request to track.chanret[.]com, where the URL path encodes a campaign ID and the recipient's base64-encoded email address as the image filename, for example hxxp://track.chanret[.]com/images/4x406rtk5/ZW1haWxAZXhhbXBsZS5jb20.jpg. That means every open hands recipient data directly to the UltraMailer tracking service, a passive data-collection risk victims will never see.
- UltraMailer's own documentation describes rotating the chanret[.]com tracking domain to a private domain when it gets blocklisted, language that reads as explicit anti-blocklist guidance. The tool is openly promoted on sinister[.]li, patched[.]to, BreachForums, and Russian-language dark web platforms under titles like "UltraMailer: Best Spamming Tool In The Market." When Infoblox reported the campaign to Mail250, the account was suspended and the campaign stopped within days. The actor returned to chanret[.]com on September 8, 2026, because UltraMailer has no abuse-reporting mechanism on its website.
- A trojanized UltraMailer installer, UltraMailer_setup_v3.6_en.exe (SHA-256: 9e1a679ca45a149d2bd681cbb8ec3b1cc3d271fad51b092a3db5e5642eb6676b), carries an embedded njRAT payload, detected by 45 of 75 vendors on VirusTotal. The installer is unsigned but bundles an authentic UltraMailer copy signed with a DUC FABULOUS CO.,LTD Sectigo certificate (thumbprint 936BB9B6A2F8E1CD149B33F4A16D8A927CD675DE), meaning spammers hunting for the bulk-mail tool may themselves be getting backdoored.
- A trojanized UltraViewer installer, UltraViewer_setup_6.6.133_vi.exe (SHA-256: 28f046d9f985e58cbc8b245b54d4179feacecc12f41e2f6594306867ce3e8727), submitted to VirusTotal on September 4, 2026, was detected by 60 of 76 vendors and attributed to Win32.Comet.A, also known as DarkKometa. It drops its payload to C:\ProgramData\Synaptics\Synaptics.exe, impersonating the Synaptics touchpad driver. Third-party research by Hexastrike links the DUC FABULOUS CO.,LTD certificate used across these samples to the Chinese 🇨🇳 threat actor Silver Fox, though Infoblox could not independently confirm the certificate was stolen.
- Infoblox observed connections to ultraviewer[.]net from as many as 30% of their customers on some days, which reflects just how broadly this remote-access tool is deployed and how large the potential abuse surface is. qbcares[.]com is listed in the report as a QuickBooks lookalike example domain.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt your environment for Synaptics.exe running from C:\ProgramData\Synaptics\ as a process masquerading as a driver, and for outbound connections to track.chanret[.]com, ultraviewer[.]net, and ultramailer[.]org. Inspect email logs for GET requests containing base64-encoded addresses routed through chanret[.]com tracking pixels. Check endpoints for UltraViewer or UltraMailer installers signed with the DUC FABULOUS CO.,LTD certificate. The two SHA-256 hashes and additional IOCs are in the Infoblox report. If UltraViewer has no business justification in your environment, DNS or firewall blocks on ultraviewer[.]net will reduce the attack surface without waiting for an incident.

item.title: Hackers Exploited Cisco SD-WAN Flaw to Plant Malware Built to Steal Encryption Keys
item.description:
CVE-2026-20127 (CVSS 10.0): Custom malware KeyDrift planted on Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controllers to steal AES-256 encryption keys passing between routers, linked to infrastructure overlapping with Volt Typhoon activity.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-20127 is a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass affecting Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller (formerly vSmart), Manager (formerly vManage), and Validator (formerly vBond), on-premises and hosted, including FedRAMP environments. Exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to gain administrative privileges. Cisco confirmed limited exploitation in the wild. Volt Typhoon, per Lumen, was exploiting this flaw by late 2025 and continued after Cisco's February disclosure. No workaround eliminates the flaw; port-restricting 22 and 830 to known controller IPs is a partial interim measure only, and it does not remove malware already present.
- KeyDrift's architecture is purpose-built for key theft at the control plane. The component LittleFilch hooks into vdaemon, the process handling encrypted SD-WAN control connections, and reads control messages after decryption. It extracts IP addresses and a 32-byte field that Talos assesses is AES-256 key material, encrypts the collection with RSA, and writes it to /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin. A settings file at /var/tmp/vdaemon.conf specifies a UDP exfiltration destination and is deleted after a single read, which is why Talos could not recover it. Whether any keys were successfully exfiltrated is unknown.
- Persistence and injection follow a deliberate masquerade pattern. Modified runit scripts under /etc/sv/sshd/ launch the loader script conf_sshd before the real SSH server. conf_sshd writes vdaemon PIDs to /tmp/system-vdaemon, then rsshd injects PolyFlame (libdssl[.]so) into those processes. PolyFlame runs entirely in memory inside vdaemon and functions as a TinyShell-style backdoor and relay. It accepts commands embedded in SD-WAN control traffic and contains no hardcoded C2 address, complicating network-level detection. On Validators, a fake compiled binary aaamgrd under /etc/sv/aaamgr/ impersonates the real Python-based aaamgr component. The group also performed timestomping, copying timestamps and permissions from legitimate files onto malicious ones to blend modification times.
- Talos attributes this activity to UAT-11473, targeting space and satellite services, defense and aerospace, and policy research. Infrastructure "overlaps considerably" with Silent Train, the SOHO/IoT botnet Lumen associates with Volt Typhoon. Talos does not equate UAT-11473 with Volt Typhoon directly, and the relationship between UAT-11473 and UAT-8616 (the February exploitation cluster) is not stated. The Talos report does not include file hashes, domains, or IP IOCs for KeyDrift.
Practitioner takeaway: Start by checking /var/log/auth.log for "Accepted publickey for vmanage-admin" entries from unrecognized IPs, the exploitation indicator Cisco specifies. Run request admin-tech on each control component before opening a TAC case and re-scan those files using the Check Bug Applicability feature for bug CSCws52722. On compromised devices, audit /etc/sv/ for unexpected service directories (specifically /etc/sv/aaamgr/), inspect the run script under /etc/sv/sshd/ for conf_sshd references, and check for libdssl[.]so and libcommon[.]so. Because upgrading does not confirmed-clear existing implants and key replacement guidance is absent from Talos's advice, treat any positive finding as a full IR event. Talos released Snort rules 67387-67416 (Snort 2, disabled by default for subscriber sets) and 7:44-7:73 (Snort 3) for KeyDrift C2 detection on October 28. Rules 65938 and 65958 cover the CVE itself. US 🇺🇸 federal civilian agencies are under CISA's February 25 emergency directive: report root compromise to CISA and rebuild Controller, Manager, and Validator from patched images.

item.title: Hugging Face malware campaign returns to hijack GPUs for crypto mining
item.description:
Malicious Hugging Face model repositories return days after takedown, abusing trust_remote_code to deploy cryptominers and reverse shells on GPU inference servers, with one model reaching 28,412 downloads before removal.
Key findings:
- Pluto Security identified 31 malicious repositories across seven Hugging Face accounts, published in two waves since September. The models pose as Qwen2 test checkpoints and specifically target GPU hosts running self-hosted inference servers like Xinference and GPUStack. Rather than exploiting pickle deserialization or poisoned weights, the campaign abuses Hugging Face's trust_remote_code option, which executes a model's bundled Python code the moment a user loads it. Code runs before any model inference begins, so the attacker foothold is established silently at load time.
- The primary payload installs a cryptocurrency miner disguised as a Linux system process, includes a watchdog that restarts it if killed, and evicts competing miners from the machine. Some variants also open a reverse shell for direct attacker access. A model pushed hours after the first-wave takedown added a container escape script capable of taking over the underlying host. The operator's wallet received roughly $5,000 in Pearl (PRL) cryptocurrency, and the mining infrastructure was still active on pools after the repositories were removed.
- A second wave of 19 repositories appeared within days under new accounts. The flagship model scanned clean through Hugging Face's antivirus and partner tooling from Protect AI and JFrog, collecting 28,412 downloads while evading detection. A near-identical copy uploaded October 25 by account htt0118 was still live at time of reporting and BleepingComputer confirmed it carries the same miner and reverse shell. Pluto attributes the campaign to a financially motivated, Chinese 🇨🇳 speaking operator based on Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳 code comments, C2 infrastructure on Alibaba Cloud, and activity timing consistent with late-night hours in China 🇨🇳.
- Separately, Air Security flagged GitHub repository SolanaUpdateTools/solana-starter-kit, live since November 2025 with 286 stars, that positions itself as a top AI coding agent search result for Solana development. Its README contains a single PowerShell one-liner that assembles a URL from fragments at developer-update[.]app and fetches a script into memory. That script installs NetSupport Manager configured to beacon to maxwintodaybtc[.]com and establishes persistence at every login. A fake error message tells the user or agent to retry in 72 hours, designed to pass as a routine service hiccup. Air links this to a known NetSupport RAT operator previously tracked by eSentire.
Takeaway: Any system that loaded a Hugging Face model with trust_remote_code enabled in the last several months should be treated as fully compromised, not merely mined. Killing the miner process is insufficient. Hunt for unexpected processes masquerading as Linux system services, outbound connections to mining pools, and unauthorized reverse shell activity. Check for container escape artifacts if the host runs a shared GPU cluster. Rotate all credentials that machine could have accessed. For the Solana kit exposure, look for NetSupport Manager persistence and outbound connections to maxwintodaybtc[.]com. IOCs for both campaigns are in Pluto's and Air Security's respective reports.

Its README contains a single PowerShell one-liner that assembles a URL from fragments at developer-update[.]app and fetches a script into memory. That script installs NetSupport Manager configured to beacon to maxwintodaybtc[.]com and establishes persistence at every login. A fake error message tells the user or agent to retry in 72 hours, designed to pass as a routine service hiccup. Air links this to a known NetSupport RAT operator previously tracked by eSentire.

Takeaway: Any system that loaded a Hugging Face model with trust_remote_code enabled in the last several months should be treated as fully compromised, not merely mined. Killing the miner process is insufficient. Hunt for unexpected processes masquerading as Linux system services, outbound connections to mining pools, and unauthorized reverse shell activity. Check for container escape artifacts if the host runs a shared GPU cluster. Rotate all credentials that machine could have accessed. For the Solana kit exposure, look for NetSupport Manager persistence and outbound connections to maxwintodaybtc[.]com. IOCs for both campaigns are in Pluto's and Air Security's respective reports.

item.title: VAPOR PANDA Uses AI-Driven ARTEX to Scale a Global Espionage Campaign
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 APT VAPOR PANDA weaponizes the ARTEX agentic AI framework alongside DeepSeek to hit 200+ organizations across 14 countries in 11 days, deploying the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor and scaling espionage at a pace no manual operation could match.
Key details:
- Starting October 17, 2026, a single ARTEX controller linked to VAPOR PANDA infrastructure directed simultaneous intrusions against foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East; 19 U.S. 🇺🇸 organizations spanning pharma, semiconductor, defense, nuclear, and finance; and telecom providers in the U.S. 🇺🇸, Belgium 🇧🇪, and the Philippines 🇵🇭. CrowdStrike OverWatch confirmed post-exploitation at nine organizations. ARTEX transcripts recovered from an inadvertently exposed controller show the operator issuing instructions in Chinese 🇨🇳, timestamped in China 🇨🇳 Standard Time, labeled 【人类指令】 ("human instruction"), with commands to write web shells, extract domain admin passwords, and map endpoint sensor coverage.
- The attack chains were multi-path and adaptive. At one U.S. 🇺🇸 pharma org, the agent chained an unsigned SAML assertion (T1606.002) with an XXE flaw (T1190) to query the cloud Instance Metadata Service (T1552.005), obtaining a role with command-execution reach over thousands of instances. At a second pharma org, the agent deployed web shells (T1505.003), abused an unauthenticated orchestration service for container root access, read LAPS passwords (T1555), and used resource-based constrained delegation to impersonate a privileged account (T1134.001). Against a Greek 🇬🇷 government entity, the operator fed the agent a 2022 mail server directory export containing unrotated authentication keys; the agent forged an admin token (T1606), read mailboxes (T1114.002), and pivoted internally via leaked VPN configs (T1078, T1133). Planning agents consumed roughly 1.4 billion input tokens in a single intrusion, indicating enormous automated throughput across the full operation.
- BLOODALCHEMY, a backdoor first documented in October 2023, was deployed at a Middle East-based interior ministry and a Latin America-based foreign ministry. Delivery used DLL hijacking (T1574.001): a legitimate GameHook binary was renamed svchost.exe (T1036.005) to load graphics-hook-filter64.dll, which decrypted the payload graphics-hook_config.bin. The implant's internal project path is D:\ProjectX\Merman_New\. C2 domains: nginxmysql[.]com (45.153.126[.]223), sqlserver-sqlite[.]com (89.46.234[.]50), www.ddduuuppp[.]com (192.121.47[.]20). Hashes for all three files are in the IOC table in the report. C2 traffic was routed through Tor, SOCKS proxies, and a compromised relay (T1090.003), and tunneled via Chisel and SoftEther (T1572).
- Sensor evasion was baked directly into the agentic workflow. The operator instructed agents to "find Windows machines in the domain without Falcon, judging by tasklist and folder listings" (T1518.001), using 猎鹰, PRC red-team slang for the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor. This means unprotected hosts are being systematically identified and prioritized for follow-on activity at machine speed, not discovered opportunistically by a human operator.
Practitioner takeaway: hunt for ARTEX artifacts directly. The report specifies: command-line parameters containing artx or artex strings, artx-prefixed cloud role names, art18- administration-command comments in cloud logs, and the directory C:\ProgramData\artx5v\. Also audit for the BLOODALCHEMY triad: svchost.exe with a hash mismatch against the legitimate binary, graphics-hook-filter64.dll, and graphics-hook_config.bin in the same path. Rotate any signing keys, preauthentication keys, or service credentials that appeared in historical directory exports or backup data, including keys from 2022 or earlier. Enforce SAML signature validation and IMDSv2 now. IOCs and the full ATT&CK technique table are in the CrowdStrike report.
